text: Before building anything, write the proposal — a short document that forces you to commit to a specific hypothesis, method, and scope before you've sunk any time into code. This lesson gives you the structure and a worked example to compare your own draft against.

This lesson covers the six sections a capstone proposal needs and what each is for, why writing the proposal before coding catches problems that are expensive to catch later, a worked proposal for a reproduction-plus-extension capstone built on Chapter 2's GHZ and mitigation example, and a self-review checklist before moving to next lesson's scoping pass.

The six sections: a research question in one or two sentences; your testable, falsifiable hypothesis; a method summary naming the circuit, technique, hardware, and comparison; related work — the papers you're building on; deliverables, stated specifically, not 'I will investigate X'; and risks with a real fallback plan. Writing this before coding forces three decisions that are cheap to change on paper and expensive to change after you've written code: exactly what you're measuring, what you're comparing against, and what done looks like.

In the worked proposal, the hypothesis states that zero-noise extrapolation will increase measured GHZ fidelity at both three and five qubits, but the improvement will be smaller at five qubits, because larger circuits accumulate more noise for the same mitigation technique to correct. The deliverables are specific: a reproduction report for the three-qubit result, a comparison table and plot at both qubit counts, a final written report, and a presentation.

Before moving on, self-review your own draft: does the hypothesis section actually use the testable, falsifiable template from earlier, or is it still vague? Does the method summary name a specific device, not just 'a quantum computer'? Does the deliverables section name a specific figure or table, not just 'results'? And does the risks section name a real, specific risk with a real, specific fallback, not a generic 'it might not work'?

Next lesson stress-tests your proposal's scope specifically — because a well-written proposal can still be unfinishable, and scope failure, not technical difficulty, is the most common reason capstones don't get completed.
